drugs.name: maropitant (injectable)
notes: 1. Indication and dose for each indication
Injectable acute vomiting (dog+cat, label): 1 mg/kg SC or IV (IV 1–2 min) once daily ≤5 days. Dog SC ≥2 mo; SC/IV ≥4 mo. Cat ≥4 mo. (Plumb 10th pp.799–802.)
Dog PO acute vomiting: 2 mg/kg PO SID; ≥2 mo; 5 days if 2–7 mo, until ceases if older. (Plumb 10th p.801.)
Dog PO motion sickness: 8 mg/kg PO SID ≤2 days; ≥4 mo; empty stomach or small food — no full meal before travel. (Plumb 10th p.801.)
Cat PO/SC extra-label: 1 mg/kg SC or PO. iCatCare CKD 2026: 1 mg/kg SC/IV/PO q24h. Do NOT use Plumb CKD 4 mg/cat as mg/kg. Dog tabs in cats = extra-label; inj labelled for cats. (Plumb pp.801–802.)
Active vomiting: prefer injectable. Strengths (Plumb p.802): Cerenia inj 10 mg/mL; tabs 16/24/60/160 mg. Stock often Prevomax 10 mg/mL + Cerenia 16/24 mg. (Plumb 10th p.799.)
2. Major adverse effects
SC pain/swelling — refrigerate to reduce pain. Motion-sickness dose: pretravel vomiting, hypersalivation. (Plumb 10th pp.799–801.)

Dogs/cats: lethargy, anorexia, diarrhea (dogs), anaphylaxis, ataxia, tremors, dyspnea, convulsions; cats also hypersalivation, fever. IV+isoflurane: further ↓BP; acepromazine hypotension. QT prolongation. (Plumb 10th pp.799–800.)
3. Major interactions with other drugs
Ca-channel blockers (amlodipine, diltiazem, verapamil): UK label — do not combine. (Plumb 10th p.800.)

CYP3A/CYP2D inhibitors (ketoconazole, erythromycin, fluoxetine, etc.): may ↓ metabolism. Protein-bound drugs (NSAIDs, anticoagulants): monitor. QT-prolonging agents (cisapride, sotalol): avoid. (Plumb 10th p.800.)
Pantoprazole: precipitation in same IV line; do not mix in same syringe. Interactions not thoroughly investigated. (Plumb 10th pp.800–802.)
4. Contraindications for what kinds of patients
Not evaluated in GI obstruction or toxin ingestion. Hepatic dysfunction: caution; consider 50% ↓dose. (Plumb 10th p.799.)

Cardiac + antiarrhythmics: safe use not reported (QT). Breeding/pregnant/lactating: safety not established. Motion-sickness dose: caution <11 wk (bone marrow hypoplasia); client — do not give <8 wk. (Plumb 10th pp.799–801.)
5. Earliest age to use the drug
Dog tabs: acute vomiting ≥2 mo; motion sickness ≥4 mo. Dog inj: SC ≥2 mo; SC/IV ≥4 mo. Cat inj ≥4 mo. Extra-label cat PO: no separate age floor beyond inj label/iCatCare. (Plumb 10th pp.799–802.)
6. Any special instructions
Refrigerate injectable; inject promptly (↓ SC pain). IV over 1–2 min. Motion sickness: ~2 h before travel with small food; do not wrap pills tightly in snacks. (Plumb 10th pp.799–801.)
Give before chemo for best prevention. If vomiting persists, re-evaluate. Dog PO > SC (lower oral bioavailability). (Plumb 10th p.799.)
7. Can the drug be crushed or split
Crushing tablets: Not stated in available sources.
Splitting: ½ or ¼ OK; wrap remainder in foil. Halved out of blister: no potency loss over 48 h. Scoring marks: Not stated in available sources. (Plumb 10th p.801.)
8. Others
NK-1 antagonist (Cerenia®, Prevomax®). Keep Plumb CKD 4 mg/cat (NOT mg/kg) separate from 1 mg/kg regimens. Human skin/eye exposure precautions. (Plumb 10th pp.799–801.)
drugs.source: Plumb's Veterinary Drug Handbook, 10th Edition — Maropitant monograph pp. 799–801 (cats continue p. 802). Dog inj 1 mg/kg SC (± IV); cat inj 1 mg/kg SC or IV q24h ≤5 days. Chemistry/Synonyms lists Cerenia® and Prevomax®.

drugs.name: doxycycline (tablets)
notes: 1. Indication and dose for each indication
Respiratory dog+cat: 5 mg/kg PO q12h OR 10 mg/kg PO q24h. B. bronchiseptica, Mycoplasma, C. felis (cats); >4 wk without enamel discoloration. (ISCAID respiratory 2017 Table 2.)
UTI reserved dog+cat: 5 mg/kg PO q12h only (low urine excretion). (ISCAID UTI 2019.)
Canine pyoderma second-choice: 5 mg/kg PO q12h OR 10 mg/kg PO q24h; AST for doxycycline specifically. (ISCAID pyoderma 2025 Table 15.)
Plumb extra-label support (not display source): often 5 mg/kg q12h or 10 mg/kg q24h. (Plumb 10th pp.436–437.)
2. Major adverse effects

Common: vomiting, diarrhea, anorexia; food may help. Esophagitis/strictures — especially cats. ↑ ALT/ALP common; often not clinically significant in dogs. Do not give IM/SC. (Plumb 10th pp.433, 435–436.)
3. Major interactions with other drugs

Al/Ca/Mg, zinc, bismuth, kaolin/pectin: separate 1–2 h. Oral iron: 3 h before or 2 h after. Sucralfate OK if 2 h after doxy. PPIs ↓ bioavailability; phenobarbital ↓ half-life; warfarin — may need adjustment. (Plumb 10th pp.435–436.)
Client: avoid multivitamins/Ca/antacids/laxatives 2 h before/after; food without iron or dairy for GI upset. (Plumb 10th p.437.)
4. Contraindications for what kinds of patients

Hypersensitivity. Pregnancy/pediatrics: class skeletal/teeth risks — benefits vs risks (doxy much less likely). Nursing: dams should not nurse. Hepatic dysfunction (dogs): caution. Renal insufficiency: CAN use. (Plumb 10th pp.433, 435.)
5. Earliest age to use the drug
ISCAID: kittens/puppies >4 weeks without enamel discoloration. Plumb: no separate numeric earliest age; bone/teeth effects much less likely than other tetracyclines. (Plumb 10th pp.433, 435.)
6. Any special instructions
Cats: never dry-pill; follow with ≥5 mL water or food (Plumb); ISCAID: lubricant + water / pill treat / ≥2 mL liquid / food. (Plumb 10th pp.435–437; ISCAID.)
GI upset: small food without iron/dairy; separate cations 2 h. Complete full course. Prefer commercial oral liquid vs unstable compounded aqueous. (Plumb 10th pp.437–438.)
7. Can the drug be crushed or split
Explicit crush/split scored-tablet recommendation: Not stated in available sources.

Compounded slurry OK for cats. Tabs mixed with water/foods lose >10% potency after 24 h; compounded aqueous: refrigerate, light-protect, use ≤7 days. Paste = same mg/kg as tabs (avoids dry-pill). (Plumb 10th pp.436–438.)
8. Others
No FDA-approved systemic vet doxy — typically extra-label. Preferred tetracycline if azotemic. MDR1: no dose change. Paste ≠ compounded-aqueous stability assurance. (Plumb 10th pp.434–435, 438.)
drugs.source: ISCAID Antimicrobial use Guidelines for Treatment of Respiratory Tract Disease in Dogs and Cats (Lappin et al. J Vet Intern Med 2017;31:279–294) Table 2 — Doxycycline 5 mg/kg, PO, q12h Or 10 mg/kg, PO, q24h. DOI 10.1111/jvim.14627; PMC5354050. Supporting: ISCAID UTI 2019 (Weese et al. Vet J) 5 mg/kg PO q12h reserved; ISCAID canine pyoderma 2025 (Loeffler et al.) Table 15 second-choice same 5 q12h / 10 q24h (dogs). Plumb's 10th not verified in-hand for this entry.

drugs.name: prednisolone (tablets — dog)
notes: 1. Indication and dose for each indication
Anti-inflammatory (calculator default) — dog: 0.5–1 mg/kg PO once daily; not to exceed 40 mg/dog (NOT mg/kg) in large-breed dogs. Same total daily dose may be SID or divided BID. (Plumb 10th p.1061.)
Anti-inflammatory — cat: prednisoLONE 1–2 mg/kg PO once daily. Prefer prednisoLONE over prednisone in cats. (Plumb 10th pp.1058, 1061.)

Immunosuppressive — dog: initial 2–4 mg/kg PO once daily; many begin 2 mg/kg and divide total dose BID. Dogs >25 kg: 50–60 mg/m² once daily may be considered. Many internists: prednisone total daily dose ≤60–80 mg regardless of weight. (Plumb 10th pp.1061–1062.)
Immunosuppressive — cat: initial prednisolone 2–8 mg/kg PO once daily; many start 4 mg/kg then divide BID. Cats generally need higher doses than dogs. (Plumb 10th p.1062.)
Other Plumb uses (not calculator default): antineoplastic; hypoadrenocorticism oral replacement much lower. (Plumb 10th p.1062.)
Tablet strengths: vet-labelled prednisoLONE 5 mg and 20 mg (hospital stock). (Plumb 10th p.1063.)
2. Major adverse effects
Long-term / high-dose / non–alternate-day: iatrogenic hyperadrenocorticism; may delay growth in young animals. (Plumb 10th p.1060.)
Dogs: PU/PD/PP; dull coat, weight gain, panting, GI signs, ↑ liver enzymes, ulceration (esp. high doses), hypercoagulability, DM activation, muscle wasting, behaviour changes. (Plumb 10th p.1060.)
Cats: often higher doses but fewer AEs; greater hyperglycemic effect; occasional PU/PD/PP, diarrhea, depression; long-term high-dose Cushingoid. (Plumb 10th p.1060.)
3. Major interactions with other drugs
NSAIDs/aspirin: ↑ GI ulcer risk with glucocorticoids. Insulin: requirements may ↑. Immunosuppressive doses: avoid live attenuated vaccines; diminished response possible. (Plumb 10th pp.1058, 1061.)

Also: K-depleting diuretics/amphotericin B (hypokalemia); enzyme inducers/inhibitors altering GC metabolism; cyclosporine; fluoroquinolones (tendinopathy); warfarin — monitor; others per monograph. (Plumb 10th p.1061.)
4. Contraindications for what kinds of patients

Systemic fungal infections (unless Addison replacement); IM if idiopathic thrombocytopenia; hypersensitivity. Caution: active infection, corneal ulcer, hyperadrenocorticism, DM, osteoporosis, CHF, hypertension, renal insufficiency; hepatic dysfunction impairs prednisone→prednisoLONE conversion. (Plumb 10th pp.1058, 1060.)
Pregnancy: may induce parturition late gestation; congenital anomalies reported. Nursing: caution — unbound GC enter milk. (Plumb 10th p.1060.)
5. Earliest age to use the drug
Numeric earliest age (weeks/months): Not stated in available sources.
Glucocorticoids can delay growth in young growing animals; monitor growth/development. (Plumb 10th pp.1060, 1063.)
6. Any special instructions

Taper / do not stop abruptly: chronic GC — taper slowly; extra GC if stressor during taper. Daily therapy >1–2 weeks → HPA suppressed — taper with alternate-day therapy (daily induction → minimum daily dose → EOD). Avoid >1 mg/kg (prednisoLONE equivalent) EOD when possible. Client: do not suddenly stop without veterinarian advice. (Plumb 10th pp.1060–1061, 1063.)

Cited sample taper (dog immunosuppressive only — not a hospital protocol): 2.2 mg/kg daily (≤60–80 mg total/day) × 3 wk → 1 mg/kg daily × 3 wk → 0.5 mg/kg daily × 3 wk → 0.5 mg/kg EOD if remission maintained. (Plumb 10th p.1062.)
Give with food. Lowest dose, shortest time. Prefer prednisoLONE in cats (and horses / severe hepatic failure). (Plumb 10th pp.1058, 1063.)
7. Can the drug be crushed or split
Crushing tablets: Not stated in available sources.
Splitting / scoring marks: Not stated in available sources.
8. Others
Same monograph: PrednisoLONE / Prednisone / PrednisoLONE Sodium Succinate (pp.1058–1063). Intermediate-acting; biologic half-life ~12–36 h.
Calculator is PO tablets only. High-dose not supported for hemorrhagic/hypovolemic shock, head/spinal trauma, or sepsis. (Plumb 10th pp.1059, 1061.)
Lab: may ↑ cholesterol/urine glucose, ↓ K; suppress TSH/T3/T4; skin-test withdrawal often 14 days. (Plumb 10th p.1061.)
drugs.source: Plumb’s Veterinary Drug Handbook, 10th Edition — PrednisoLONE/Prednisone/PrednisoLONE Sodium Succinate monograph pp.1058–1063.

Long-term / high-dose / non–alternate-day: iatrogenic hyperadrenocorticism; may delay growth in young animals. (Plumb 10th p.1060.)
Dogs: PU/PD/PP; dull coat, weight gain, panting, GI signs, ↑ liver enzymes, ulceration (esp. high doses), hypercoagulability, DM activation, muscle wasting, behaviour changes. (Plumb 10th p.1060.)
Cats: often higher doses but fewer AEs; greater hyperglycemic effect; occasional PU/PD/PP, diarrhea, depression; long-term high-dose Cushingoid. (Plumb 10th p.1060.)
3. Major interactions with other drugs
NSAIDs/aspirin: ↑ GI ulcer risk with glucocorticoids. Insulin: requirements may ↑. Immunosuppressive doses: avoid live attenuated vaccines; diminished response possible. (Plumb 10th pp.1058, 1061.)

Also: K-depleting diuretics/amphotericin B (hypokalemia); enzyme inducers/inhibitors altering GC metabolism; cyclosporine; fluoroquinolones (tendinopathy); warfarin — monitor; others per monograph. (Plumb 10th p.1061.)
4. Contraindications for what kinds of patients

Systemic fungal infections (unless Addison replacement); IM if idiopathic thrombocytopenia; hypersensitivity. Caution: active infection, corneal ulcer, hyperadrenocorticism, DM, osteoporosis, CHF, hypertension, renal insufficiency; hepatic dysfunction impairs prednisone→prednisoLONE conversion. (Plumb 10th pp.1058, 1060.)
Pregnancy: may induce parturition late gestation; congenital anomalies reported. Nursing: caution — unbound GC enter milk. (Plumb 10th p.1060.)
5. Earliest age to use the drug
Numeric earliest age (weeks/months): Not stated in available sources.
Glucocorticoids can delay growth in young growing animals; monitor growth/development. (Plumb 10th pp.1060, 1063.)
6. Any special instructions

Taper / do not stop abruptly: chronic GC — taper slowly; extra GC if stressor during taper. Daily therapy >1–2 weeks → HPA suppressed — taper with alternate-day therapy (daily induction → minimum daily dose → EOD). Avoid >1 mg/kg (prednisoLONE equivalent) EOD when possible. Client: do not suddenly stop without veterinarian advice. (Plumb 10th pp.1060–1061, 1063.)

Cited sample taper (dog immunosuppressive only — not a hospital protocol): 2.2 mg/kg daily (≤60–80 mg total/day) × 3 wk → 1 mg/kg daily × 3 wk → 0.5 mg/kg daily × 3 wk → 0.5 mg/kg EOD if remission maintained. (Plumb 10th p.1062.)
Give with food. Lowest dose, shortest time. Prefer prednisoLONE in cats (and horses / severe hepatic failure). (Plumb 10th pp.1058, 1063.)
7. Can the drug be crushed or split
Crushing tablets: Not stated in available sources.
Splitting / scoring marks: Not stated in available sources.
8. Others
Same monograph: PrednisoLONE / Prednisone / PrednisoLONE Sodium Succinate (pp.1058–1063). Intermediate-acting; biologic half-life ~12–36 h.
Calculator is PO tablets only. High-dose not supported for hemorrhagic/hypovolemic shock, head/spinal trauma, or sepsis. (Plumb 10th pp.1059, 1061.)
Lab: may ↑ cholesterol/urine glucose, ↓ K; suppress TSH/T3/T4; skin-test withdrawal often 14 days. (Plumb 10th p.1061.)
